findings.evidence: "items still unreturned past that window remain subject to the existing replacement-cost billing process, matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established" -- but the only pilot data given ("What the Pilot Showed") is a single aggregate "on-time-or-eventual return rate" of 94 percent vs 87 percent over the full 16-month pilot; no return-by-day-60 breakdown appears anywhere in the artifact.
findings.fix: Either report the pilot's actual return-timing data broken out around the 60-day mark, or drop the claim that the cutoff matches an established pilot pattern and justify the 60-day figure on its own terms (e.g., as an operational choice rather than a data-derived one).
findings.location: Recommendation section, third paragraph ("This recommendation applies to items returned within 60 days...")
findings.violation: TOULMIN-GROUNDS requires that a claim be attached to evidence a reader could check. This sentence asserts that a specific 60-day cutoff "matches" a pattern "the pilot data actually established," but no pilot data broken out by a 60-day return window is presented, so a reader cannot verify the match the sentence claims.

findings.evidence: "Consortium finance records show fine revenue covered under 2 percent of the annual materials budget over the last three fiscal years, and the four pilot branches absorbed the loss without a measurable change to their replacement-copy spending, so the shortfall the objection anticipates has not materialized where the policy has already been tried."
findings.fix: Add a passage addressing why full elimination rather than a partial fine reduction is recommended, e.g., by citing pilot or Tri-County brief data that distinguishes the two, or by stating why a partial-fee option was not considered viable.
findings.violation: TOULMIN-REBUTTAL requires naming and addressing the conditions the argument's own grounds leave open, including an alternative the grounds do not rule out. The pilot tested only a binary choice (full fines vs. no fines), so its grounds do not rule out whether a partial fine reduction would capture most of the return-rate and avoidance benefit while preserving more revenue. The argument answers the revenue-shortfall objection with pilot data but never raises or addresses this foreseeable partial-reduction alternative.
